## Corticosteroids in Fulminant Myocarditis Associated With Viral Infection

Florent Huang , MD; Enrico Ammirati , MD, PhD; Maharajah Ponnaiah , PhD; Santiago Montero , MD; Nadia Aïssaoui, MD, PhD; Albert Ariza Solé , MD, PhD; Martin Balik , MD, PhD; Eduardo Barge-Caballero, MD, PhD; Jeroen J.H. Bunge , MD; Hergen Buscher , MD, PhD; Clément Delmas , MD, PhD; Dirk W. Donker , MD, PhD; Christoph Fisser, MD; Guillaume Franchineau, MD; Justin Fried , MD; Francisco José Hernández-Pérez , MD, PhD; Joshua Ihle , MD; Jae-Seung Jung , MD, PhD; Teresa Lόpez-Sobrino , MD; Jamie McCanny , MD; Armand Mekontso Dessap , MD, PhD; Henrique Muglia, MD; Shinichiro Ohshimo , MD, PhD; Sunghoon Park, MD, PhD; Romain Persichini, MD; Beatriz Porral, MD; Roberto Roncon-Albuquerque Jr , MD, PhD; Alessandro Sionis , MD, PhD; Pauline Yeung Ng, MD; Alain Combes, MD, PhD; Matthieu Schmidt , MD, PhD; for the FULLMOON Study Group*

## F

ulminant myocarditis (FM) represents the most severe manifestation of acute myocarditis, characterized by profound cardiogenic shock necessitating inotropes or temporary mechanical circulatory support. The FULL- MOON study (Fulminant Myocarditis: Outcomes and Long-Term Prognosis) showed that early endomyocardial biopsy was associated with better survival without heart transplantation or left ventricular assist device, compared with delayed endomyocardial biopsy.1 An early endomyocardial biopsy could facilitate prompt histological confirmation, microbiological workup, and initiation of immunomodulatory therapies (IMT). Current guidelines caution against using IMT in confirmed viral infections to mitigate the risk of exacerbating viral replication. However, emerging data suggest that certain viruses, notably Parvovirus B19 (PVB19) and Human Herpesvirus type 6, commonly found in myocarditis, may not be direct causal agents but rather bystanders.2 Hence, our objective was to evaluate the safety of IMT in patients with FM associated with viral infection, within a large international retrospective cohort involving 36 centers. A comprehensive overview of the FULLMOON study has been previously published.1 All participating centers obtained institutional review board approval following their local regulations and adhered to the Declaration

of Helsinki. In France (the coordinating country), institutional review board approval was obtained by Hospital Foch (institutional review board-00012437 number 21-08-05). Data supporting the study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Briefly, of the entire cohort, 306 (73%) patients had proven myocarditis either by histological examination or by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, among whom 236 (77%) underwent a viral workup (91 in heart tissues and 145 in blood or respiratory tract samples). This ancillary substudy focused on the 63 patients with confirmed FM and positive viral testing (eg, if the viral polymerase chain reaction was positive in heart or respiratory tract samples irrespectively of viral load, or if the viral load was measured ≥3 log in blood tests). Their baseline characteristics, diagnosis features, in-hospital events, and outcomes are outlined in the Table. Notably, all histological analyses, except one, exhibited lymphocytic or pluricellular infiltrates. Viral polymerase chain reaction testing yielded positive results in heart samples for 19 (30%) patients, of which most were PVB19 (n=11, 58%), and in peripheral samples for the remaining 44, with Influenza viruses predominantly identified (n=19, 43%). Temporary mechanical circulatory support was required by 51 (81%) patients for a median duration of 6 (4–10) days.

Fifteen (24%) patients were treated with corticosteroids, of whom 2 received additional azathioprine and intravenous immunoglobulins, within 1 (0–2) day after admission. Corticosteroid therapy was administered either with 3 boluses of methylprednisolone 1 g/d followed by 1 mg/kg per day (n=12), 1 mg/kg per day without bolus (n=2), or 100 mg/d hydrocortisone (n=1). No significant differences were observed between patients receiving IMT (Virus+/IMT+, n=15) and those who did not (Virus+/IMT−, n=48) regarding FM severity (initial severity scores, baseline lactate levels, rates of temporary mechanical circulatory support), except for a significantly shorter duration of mechanical ventilation in the first group (9 [6–11] versus 11 [4–17] days, P=0.035). The 1-year survival rates free from heart transplantation/ left ventricular assist device were similar between both groups (80% versus 71%, respectively; log-rank test

P=0.53). Interestingly, when limited to patients with a positive heart viral workup (n=19), the 1-year survival free from heart transplantation/left ventricular assist device was significantly higher in the Virus+/IMT+ group (n=6) compared with the Virus+/IMT− group (n=13; 100% versus 38%, log-rank test P=0.021). Our study suggests that corticosteroid use in patients with FM, despite a positive viral workup, is not associated with harm and may potentially contribute to a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation. Practically, this may reassure clinicians regarding the safety of starting IMT while the microbiological workup is still ongoing. Consistent with prior studies, PVB19 was the most frequently isolated virus in heart samples.3 However, apart from Coxsackies, the pathogenicity of viruses implicated in myocarditis, particularly PVB19, remains controversial.2 Moreover, the clinical implications of virus presence in myocarditis remain uncertain since virus clearance did not correlate with improved survival.4 Future studies are needed to improve understanding of the role of viruses and their inflammatory response in the pathogenesis of FM. Our study has several limitations, primarily due to its retrospective design and small sample size. First, the microbiological evaluation relied solely on quantitative polymerase chain reaction, which may inadequately distinguish between active infections and asymptomatic viral reactivations. Second, many of our patients lacked comprehensive heart and peripheral microbiological assessments, complicating the interpretation of polymerase chain reaction results. Third, IMT protocols were not standardized between centers. In conclusion, corticosteroids seem safe in patients with FM presenting with ongoing viral replication (mainly PVB19 and Influenza viruses). Large multicenter cohorts and randomized controlled trials are necessary to confirm these hypothesis-generating observations and to evaluate the efficacy of IMT, particularly corticosteroids, in lymphocytic FM.
